newsitem.title: USA: Vermont says Sept revenues rose, but cautious.
newsitem.headline: Vermont says Sept revenues rose, but cautious.

text.p: Vermont's Secretary of Administration on Thursday cautioned that although revenues rose 4.6 percent in September and the state met its first quarter target, some "economic and revenue concerns" remained.

William Sorrell, in prepared remarks, listed a number of concerns, including some lower tax collections, predictions the Federal Reserve will raise rates in the next six to nine months, and the expected loss of more than 550 high-paying jobs at manufacturers by next September.
How the state fares for the rest of the year hinges in part on the winter ski season.

"These concerns, together with the fact that the next six months constitute the most critical tourism months of the year, cause us to remain cautious for the remaining three quarters of fiscal year 1997," he said, in prepared remarks.
The revenues that Vermont collected in September totaled $71.5 million. And receipts for the first 1997 fiscal quarter, which ended on September 30, increased 3.4 percent to $173.4 million.

Some areas produced additional funds, with personal income tax collections rising 10 percent, mainly due to a rise in estimated and withholding taxes. A $2.2 million transfer from the Lottery also helped.
This increases helped put the General Fund revenue total on target for the first quarter, an achievement Sorrell called a significant improvement over the same period last year.
But sales and use tax collections underperformed their $15.35 million target, only totaling $14.67 million, he told Reuters in an interview.

And while some categories, estate, insurance and the telephone property tax, performed well when measured against their monthly target for September, they were down about $1.3 million during the first two months of the quarter, he said.
This left the general fund a bit behind projections. "Through the first quarter of the fiscal year in the general fund we are behind where we thought we would be by about $1.6 million," Sorrell said.
However, the transporation fund is running around $1.8 million ahead of its expected results. "So we're about $200,000 ahead on a combined basis," he explained.

Vermont keeps a separate transportation fund, although these revenues support its general obligation debt, as a way of trying to ensure that the money is spent for this purpose as much as possible. The funds also are used to pay for a variety of other expenses, including some of the costs of the state police and judiciary.

Revenues for the transportation fund rose 2.6 percent to $12.1 million in September. Cumulative revenue collections for the first quarter were $34.7 million, a 2.8 percent rise over the year-ago period.
